newsitem.title: MONTSERRAT: Montserrat capital virtually destroyed by volcano.
newsitem.headline: Montserrat capital virtually destroyed by volcano.

text.p: The Soufriere Hills volcano belched more ash and hot rock on Wednesday, sending rivers of debris into Montserrat's abandoned capital where fires had burned out but streets were covered with thick volcanic ash.

Explosive eruptions showered even the "safe zone" at the north end of the troubled Caribbean island with pebbles of volcanic debris. But officials said no one had been injured by the latest activity in the rumbling mountain.

In Plymouth, about 80 percent of the buildings were damaged or destroyed by days of red-hot rockflows that touched off raging fires and filled streets with boulders and ash, government spokesman Richard Aspin said.
"It's a huge fan shape of destruction. Most buildings are either burned out or covered in debris," he said. "Ash deposits are up to four feet thick."

Fires touched off by the "pyroclastic flows" of rock, ash and hot gases razed government headquarters, the customs office, public market and other landmark buildings. The fires were allowed to burn themselves out because the town was too dangerous for firefighters, officials said.
Plymouth once was a quaint, bustling colonial town of 5,000 and the centre of the British colony's social and commercial life.

But the volcano, which roared to life in July 1995, has forced its evacuation three times, the last in April 1996. Government officials said the town was virtually destroyed and a new capital likely would be built in the north.
"We haven't used the city for so long now," Aspin said.
Sirens rang out around midday on Wednesday, warning residents that scientists expected another explosive eruption soon.
Much of the island's central region remained under an evacuation order issued on Tuesday, with residents crowded into public shelters and friends' homes in the north.
The volcano's eruptions during the past four days sent clouds of ash as high as 40,000 feet (12,000 metres), dusting the islands of Nevis and Antigua more than 25 miles (40 km) away.
